implementation_notes: Go 1.21's slices package is the standard-library form: DeleteFunc takes a slice and a predicate, compacts the survivors forward in one pass, returns the shortened slice, and clears the vacated tail so removed references do not stay reachable. The erase-remove pair cannot exist as it does in C++ because a Go slice is (pointer, length, capacity): the delete step is just re-slicing to the write index, which is why one library function can own both halves. Prefer it whenever the module's go directive allows 1.21 or newer; slices.Delete is the by-range equivalent, and the standard library documents that one bulk call is cheaper than deleting one element at a time.
pitfalls: DeleteFunc compacts the backing array and returns a new slice header: an older alias or subslice still exposes the moved data, and the previous contents are not preserved.
Forgetting the assignment (calling slices.DeleteFunc(xs, pred) alone) discards the shortened length, so the original header still covers the removed elements.

variants.name: two-index compaction loop (works on every Go version)
variants.idiom_name: n := 0; for _, v := range s { if keep(v) { s[n] = v; n++ } }; s = s[:n]
variants.implementation_notes: Before the slices package - and still in code that must build with older toolchains - the idiom is written out: one forward pass with a write index copying each retained element down, then a re-slice to that index. It is the same compaction DeleteFunc performs, plus the tail question: clear the removed slots yourself (clear(s[n:]) with Go 1.21's builtin, or an explicit zeroing loop before it) whenever the removed elements hold references that should become collectable. Choose the loop when the predicate must also do something with the removed value, when the write index is needed for a second array, or when the slice is a window over shared memory whose length must be adjusted by hand.
pitfalls: Deleting with append(s[:i], s[i+1:]...) inside the iteration loop is the quadratic anti-pattern - each call shifts the tail - and append may reallocate, detaching the slice from its backing array and from every alias.

Re-slicing to s[:n] keeps capacity: the array stays allocated (fine - releasing memory is a separate decision), but the removed slots must be cleared or the garbage collector keeps whatever they reference alive.
